title: The One That Passed
narrativeQuestion: Why did a demand to exclude Chinese workers become federal law, and how did Chinese communities challenge it?

chapters.title: The Sierra
chapters.claim: Nineteen years before Haymarket, three thousand Chinese workers made the same demand American labor would build a movement around, and they were already part of the labor struggle. They lost it in a week because their employer controlled the road that carried their food. This is who these workers were before any law was written about them.

chapters.title: The Sandlot
chapters.claim: This is the same July students already watched in Lecture 15. The Great Railroad Strike reached San Francisco as a sympathy rally and turned into three nights of attacks on Chinese homes and businesses. The man who came out of it with a movement had been on the other side of the line, carrying a pick handle for the committee that broke up the riot.

chapters.title: The One That Passed
chapters.claim: Five selected labor records contrast workplace defeats with federal exclusion; this is not a claim that labor never won other campaigns.

chapters.title: The First Law
chapters.claim: The Page Act is the first restrictive federal immigration law in American history, and on paper it is about trafficking. In practice it was the instrument that kept Chinese women out. A population that cannot form families does not replace itself, which is why the law that came seven years later did not need to be permanent in order to be permanent.

chapters.title: May 6, 1882
chapters.claim: Exclusion passed by more than five to one in the House and more than two to one in the Senate.

chapters.title: What The Law Did
chapters.claim: Between 1890 and 1920 the Chinese population of the United States fell by nearly half while the population of the country grew sharply. The law did not merely stop growth. It reversed it, and it kept reversing it for thirty years.

chapters.title: Rock Springs
chapters.claim: Exclusion did not calm the West. It ratified the position that Chinese workers did not belong, and the three years after 1882 were the most violent in the entire history of Chinese settlement in America. Rock Springs was one of the deadliest attacks, and its aftermath showed how the people responsible could escape prosecution.

chapters.title: The Method
chapters.claim: Rock Springs was a massacre. Tacoma was a procedure, run by elected officials, with a published deadline and an orderly march. It was copied across the West because it worked and because nobody involved was punished. Killing was not the common method. Paperwork and a deadline were.

chapters.title: Six Days
chapters.claim: The government issued a document, then cancelled the document, then refused to honor it, and the Supreme Court held unanimously that it was entitled to do all three. The case became a foundation of the broad congressional authority known as plenary power.

chapters.title: The Other Record
chapters.claim: The record of this period runs in two directions at once. Everything so far has been done to Chinese immigrants. From here the hour follows what they did, and what they did was sue. Chinese residents brought thousands of cases in American courts during exclusion, and some of what they won protects everyone in the country now.

chapters.title: One Hundred Thousand Said No
chapters.claim: This was one of the largest organized acts of civil disobedience in nineteenth century America, and almost nobody has heard of it. It was funded, coordinated, and carried out by people who were barred from citizenship, and it was a genuine gamble that failed in court.

chapters.title: The Boy From Sacramento Street
chapters.claim: Wong Kim Ark won citizenship at birth under the Fourteenth Amendment.

namedPeople.name: Wong Kim Ark

chapters.title: Sixty One Years
chapters.claim: Exclusion persisted for 61 elapsed years before repeal introduced a quota of 105.
